title: When to Start Mowing Your Lawn in Springfield, MO
excerpt: Southwest Missouri sits in the transition zone, so timing your first cut right matters. Here's how to know when your lawn is ready.
body: Springfield sits in what turf experts call the "transition zone" — too far south for purely cool-season grass and too far north for warm-season grass to thrive year-round. That mix means the right time to start mowing depends more on your grass's growth, not the date on the calendar.

For cool-season lawns (fescue, bluegrass), growth typically picks up in late March to early April once soil temperatures climb. For warm-season lawns (Bermuda, zoysia), things stay dormant and brown longer, often not greening up until late April or May.

The simplest rule: mow when the grass needs it, not on a fixed date. Once your lawn is actively growing and reaches about a third taller than your target height, it's time for the first cut. Cutting too early on dormant or stressed grass can do more harm than good.
Not sure where your lawn stands? That's exactly the kind of thing we check on the first visit before setting a mowing schedule.

title: How Often Should You Really Be Mowing?
excerpt: Weekly, bi-weekly, or something else? The right frequency depends on the season and how fast your grass is growing, not a fixed schedule.
body: The most common mowing mistake we see isn't cutting too short — it's cutting on a rigid schedule instead of a schedule that matches how fast the grass is actually growing.

During peak growing season (typically May through June in southwest Missouri), weekly mowing is usually necessary to avoid removing too much leaf blade at once. In the heat of summer or during dry spells, growth slows down and bi-weekly can be enough. In early spring and late fall, growth is slower still.

A good guideline is the "one-third rule": never remove more than a third of the grass blade height in a single cut. If you're regularly cutting off more than that, it's a sign your mowing frequency needs to catch up with your grass's growth rate.
This is exactly why we offer weekly, bi-weekly, and one-time scheduling — so your service actually matches your lawn instead of a one-size-fits-all calendar.

title: Fall Lawn Cleanup Checklist for Missouri Homeowners
excerpt: Leaves, debris, and a few key tasks now set your lawn up for a healthier spring green-up. Here's what to prioritize before winter.
body: A thick layer of wet leaves left on the lawn all winter blocks sunlight and traps moisture against the grass, which can lead to matted, damaged patches come spring. Regular leaf removal through fall is one of the highest-value things you can do for your lawn's health.
Beyond leaves, fall cleanup is a good time to clear out summer's dead annuals, cut back perennials, and pull any lingering debris out of garden beds before mulching for winter.

Fall is also the ideal window for cool-season lawns to recover from summer stress — pairing a cleanup with fall fertilization and aeration gives grass the best shot at a strong root system before winter dormancy.
We offer fall cleanup as a one-time service or bundled with a seasonal treatment plan, whichever fits your yard.

title: Fertilization Timing: A Season-by-Season Guide
excerpt: Applying the right treatment at the wrong time wastes money and misses weeds at their most vulnerable stage. Here's how the seasons break down.
body: Fertilization and weed control work best when they're timed around the plant's growth cycle, not applied on a flat monthly schedule.

Early spring (pre-emergent season) is about stopping crabgrass and other summer weeds before they germinate — this window closes fast once soil temperatures warm up. Late spring and early summer applications focus on feeding the lawn through its most active growth period.

Late summer and fall broadleaf weed treatments tend to be the most effective of the year, since perennial weeds are pulling nutrients down into their root systems and carry the treatment down with them. Fall is also prime time for a final fertilization to build root strength before winter.
A season-long program beats one-off treatments because it keeps weeds from ever getting a foothold, rather than reacting after they've already spread.

title: Why Core Aeration Matters (And When to Do It)
excerpt: Compacted soil chokes out a healthy lawn from the roots up. Here's what aeration actually does and how to know if your yard needs it.
body: Foot traffic, heavy clay soil, and mowing over the years all compact the soil underneath your lawn. Compacted soil makes it harder for water, air, and nutrients to reach the roots — even a lawn that gets fertilized regularly can struggle if the soil underneath is too dense.

Core aeration pulls small plugs of soil out of the lawn, relieving that compaction and giving roots room to grow deeper and stronger. Deeper roots mean better drought tolerance and a lawn that bounces back faster from stress.
For cool-season lawns, fall is generally the best time to aerate, since it lines up with their peak growing period. For warm-season lawns, late spring to early summer works better.
If your lawn feels hard underfoot, water tends to pool or run off instead of soaking in, or growth has been thinning despite regular care, it's worth having it checked for compaction.

title: Mulch 101: Choosing the Right Mulch for Your Beds
excerpt: Mulch does more than look tidy — it holds moisture, blocks weeds, and protects roots. Here's how to pick the right type for your landscaping.
body: Beyond curb appeal, a good layer of mulch helps beds retain moisture between waterings, suppresses weed growth by blocking sunlight, and moderates soil temperature for plant roots.

Hardwood mulch breaks down over time and adds organic matter back into the soil, making it a solid all-around choice for most garden beds. Dyed mulches hold their color longer through the season, which matters if curb appeal is a priority. Lighter materials like straw or pine needles work well around more delicate plantings.
A fresh 2-3 inch layer is usually the sweet spot — too thin and it won't suppress weeds effectively, too thick and it can actually hold too much moisture against plant stems.
Most beds benefit from a fresh top-up once a year, typically in spring before the growing season kicks into gear.
